rules.sentence: Atypical fibroxanthoma is a rare, low-grade superficial sarcoma frequently presenting as a red nodule or plaque.
Although atypical fibroxanthoma has similar histologic features to undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, it behaves less aggressively.[1][2][3][4]
Ultraviolet light appears to play a significant role since most lesions appear on the sun-exposed head and neck of White individuals.
Genetic factors also contribute to the development of atypical fibroxanthoma since it shares genetic alterations with undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcomas, including chromosome 9p and 13q deletions.
Other possible risk factors for atypical fibroxanthoma include trauma to the skin, radiation therapy, and immunosuppression (eg, diabetes, human immunodeficiency virus, organ transplant).[5][6][7][8]
Atypical fibroxanthomas are most commonly seen on the head and neck of older White individuals.
Trunk and limb lesions appear more commonly in younger patients (mean age 39) than head and neck lesions in the elderly (mean age 69).
Results from a review of 171 cases in Western Australia found a patient age range of 41 to 97 years old (median age 74), with 76% of the tumors occurring in men.
Atypical fibroxanthoma has also been reported in patients as young as 13 with predisposing disorders such as Li-Fraumeni syndrome and xeroderma pigmentosum.
The incidence increases in immunosuppressed populations, with an estimated 78 per 100,000 patients with a transplantation.
